prompt_c2:
You are a streetscape inventory annotator. Look ONLY at the uploaded streetscape image.
Return JSON ONLY. No markdown, no commentary, no reasoning.
 Task: record what is visible in the scene. Do not score, do not give design advice.
 Schema:
{
"road_type": "highway|arterial|neighborhood_street|alley|plaza|unclear",
"elements": {
"sidewalk": "true|false|unclear",
"bike_lane": "true|false|unclear",
"seating": "true|false|unclear",
"shade_trees": "none|few|many|unclear",
"curb_ramp": "true|false|unclear",
"tactile_paving": "true|false|unclear",
"pedestrian_crossing": "true|false|unclear",
"street_lighting": "true|false|unclear",
"greenery": "none|low|medium|high|unclear",
"vehicle_traffic": "none|light|heavy|unclear",
"bus_stop": "true|false|unclear"
},
"issues": ["no_seating", "little_shade", "no_bike_lane", "poor_accessibility", "narrow_sidewalk", "no_crossing", "high_traffic_exposure"],
"brief": "One or two English sentences describing the visible street scene."
}
 Rules:
- If an element is not clearly visible, use "unclear". Do not guess.
- "issues" may only list problems that are visible. Use [] if none.
- "brief" must mention concrete objects (sidewalk, trees, lanes, benches, ramps, etc.).

Physical infra- structure, e.g., traffic lights and raised medians (traffic islands) reduce vehicle–pedestrian collision frequency and severity (King, Carnegie, & Ewing, 2003; Stipancic, Miranda-Moreno, Strauss, & Labbe, 2020). But although physical crossing infrastructure that increases pedestrian safety can be implemented relatively cost-efficiently during the initial building of roads, the associated costs for the retroactive installation of physical road crossing infrastructure often leads to a preference for painted crosswalk markings (Stoker et al., 2015). In comparison to physical infrastructure, traditional, painted crosswalks can be installed with little resources. However, studies show that traditional marked crosswalks have little positive impact on pedestrian safety (Retting, Ferguson, & McCartt, 2003), and even increase pedestrian crash rates for some road environments (Zegeer, Stewart, Huang, & Lagerwey, 2001). In contrast to tradi- tional crosswalks, innovative crosswalk designs have more positive effects on pedestrian crash risk. High-visibility crosswalks, which use larger painted areas significantly increase pedestrian safety (Feldman, Manzi, & Mitman, 2010; Fitzpatrick, Chrysler, Iragavarapu, & Park, 2011; Guo, & Boyle, 2022; Pulugurtha, Vasudevan, Nambisan, & Dangeti, 2012; Sarwar et al., 2017). 1.1. 3D crosswalks The “3D zebra crossing” / “3D crosswalk” is a relatively new category of crosswalks which has not been investigated in depth for its effect on safety perceptions by road users. This type of crosswalk uses optical illusions to provoke the perception of a three-dimensional crosswalk from a vehicle driver’s perspective, even though the crosswalk markings are painted flat on the road. I.e., there is a dif- ference between the visual percept of road users (what they perceive) and the visual stimuli (reality). 3D crosswalks have been painted in several pilot projects around the world (e.g., in Aarhus, Denmark (Eurocities, 2021); Chiang Mai, Thailand (Pichayapan, Kaew- moracharoen, Peansara, & Nanthavisit, 2020); ´ Isafjo¨rður, Iceland (Iceland Magazine, 2017); or Montr´eal, Canada (Woods, 2018)). The 3D illusion can take the form of the crossing lines, seemingly floating above the road, or an illusionary cliff can be painted, giving the illusion of a trench in the road. A visualization of a trench illusion crosswalk is presented in Fig. 1. The evocation of depth through the painting of a flat, two-dimensional picture is categorized as a trompe l’oeil illusion (English: deceive the eye illusion) (Wade, & Hughes, 1999). As a city streetscape evaluation expert, please analyze the uploaded streetscape image based on the specified persona perspective and evaluation indicators, and return a JSON result.
 Persona Selection
Road User Type
- All Road Users
- Pedestrians
- Cyclists
- Drivers
Socially Vulnerable Groups
- All Social Groups
- Persons with Disabilities
- Adolescents (<18)
- Older Adults (≥60)
Current Selection:
All Road Users; All Social Groups
 Indicator Selection
Justice
- Equity
- Fairness
- Accessibility
Safety
Livability
Sustainability
Aesthetics
Comfort
- Thermal Comfort
- Physical Comfort
- Psychological Comfort
Walkability
Bikeability
Selected Indicators:
Justice; Safety; Livability; Sustainability; Aesthetics; Comfort; Walkability
 1. Evaluation Dimensions
Justice: Analyze whether the environment fairly distributes spatial resources, including Equity (rationality of asset distribution), Fairness (non-discriminatory rules), and Accessibility (barrier-free physical design).
Comfort: Analyze physical perception at a micro-scale, including Thermal Comfort (shade/vegetation), Physical Comfort (paving/seating), and Psychological Comfort (noise/crowding).
Core Indicators: Safety, Livability, Sustainability, Aesthetics, Walkability, and Bikeability.
 2. Persona Perspective Requirements:
The analysis must strictly adhere to the persona's characteristics. For example:
Persons with Disabilities: Focus on curb ramps, continuity of tactile paving (blind tracks), and physical obstacles.
Elderly: Focus on resting facilities, slope gradients, and summer shade.
Teenagers: Focus on traffic calming measures and social surveillance (Eyes on the street).
 3. How to use the image vs retrieved knowledge:
- The IMAGE is the primary evidence. Score only what is visible or reasonably inferable from the photo.
- Section 6 provides retrieved guidelines and research. Use them to interpret the image (what the scene should provide for this persona/indicators), not to invent objects that are not in the photo.
- If retrieved text conflicts with the image, trust the image and say so in the explanation.
- Explanations must cite specific visible objects (benches, ramps, tree shade, lane markings, etc.). When a guideline is used, briefly connect it to those objects.
 4. Output Format Requirements (Return JSON ONLY, no extra text):

Physical infra- structure, e.g., traffic lights and raised medians (traffic islands) reduce vehicle–pedestrian collision frequency and severity (King, Carnegie, & Ewing, 2003; Stipancic, Miranda-Moreno, Strauss, & Labbe, 2020). But although physical crossing infrastructure that increases pedestrian safety can be implemented relatively cost-efficiently during the initial building of roads, the associated costs for the retroactive installation of physical road crossing infrastructure often leads to a preference for painted crosswalk markings (Stoker et al., 2015). In comparison to physical infrastructure, traditional, painted crosswalks can be installed with little resources. However, studies show that traditional marked crosswalks have little positive impact on pedestrian safety (Retting, Ferguson, & McCartt, 2003), and even increase pedestrian crash rates for some road environments (Zegeer, Stewart, Huang, & Lagerwey, 2001). In contrast to tradi- tional crosswalks, innovative crosswalk designs have more positive effects on pedestrian crash risk. High-visibility crosswalks, which use larger painted areas significantly increase pedestrian safety (Feldman, Manzi, & Mitman, 2010; Fitzpatrick, Chrysler, Iragavarapu, & Park, 2011; Guo, & Boyle, 2022; Pulugurtha, Vasudevan, Nambisan, & Dangeti, 2012; Sarwar et al., 2017). 1.1. 3D crosswalks The “3D zebra crossing” / “3D crosswalk” is a relatively new category of crosswalks which has not been investigated in depth for its effect on safety perceptions by road users. This type of crosswalk uses optical illusions to provoke the perception of a three-dimensional crosswalk from a vehicle driver’s perspective, even though the crosswalk markings are painted flat on the road. I.e., there is a dif- ference between the visual percept of road users (what they perceive) and the visual stimuli (reality). 3D crosswalks have been painted in several pilot projects around the world (e.g., in Aarhus, Denmark (Eurocities, 2021); Chiang Mai, Thailand (Pichayapan, Kaew- moracharoen, Peansara, & Nanthavisit, 2020); ´ Isafjo¨rður, Iceland (Iceland Magazine, 2017); or Montr´eal, Canada (Woods, 2018)). The 3D illusion can take the form of the crossing lines, seemingly floating above the road, or an illusionary cliff can be painted, giving the illusion of a trench in the road. A visualization of a trench illusion crosswalk is presented in Fig. 1. The evocation of depth through the painting of a flat, two-dimensional picture is categorized as a trompe l’oeil illusion (English: deceive the eye illusion) (Wade, & Hughes, 1999). Paths and paved areas in roadside green spaces shall meet the following requirements: 1. The material and thickness of the paving surface layer shall be coordinated with the road greening style and use function, and integrated with sponge city design. Ecological permeable materials should be used where possible, with anti-slip functions, and polished surface materials shall not be used. 2. Traffic-function roads The sides of traffic-function roads are mainly non-open interfaces, with relatively few non-traffic activities, and the paved areas mainly serve traffic distribution functions. Paving design shall implement the concepts of safety, health, comfort, and people-oriented design. Figure 1.4-2 Example of paving for traffic-function roads B. Living-service roads The activity groups on living-service roads include residents and workers around the road, as well as people from other areas who come for shopping and strolling. In terms of paving materials, color, texture, and grain, attention shall be paid to people’s perceptions, and localized creative design shall be applied to road entrances to enrich the walking experience. Road design should focus on creating a historical and cultural atmosphere. The paving materials and texture shall be integrated with the surrounding environment.
